summary: Palau admits visitors of nearly every nationality with a free 30-day entry permit issued on arrival, while US, Micronesian and Marshallese citizens enter freely under the Compact of Free Association. Everyone pays the USD 100 Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee and signs the Palau Pledge stamped into their passport.

fee.notes: Approximate. The Bureau of Immigration charges a per-extension fee, commonly quoted around USD 50 for each additional 30 days. Confirm the current amount at the office in Koror.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months on arrival, with a clear page for the entry permit and the Palau Pledge stamp.

vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required only if you are arriving from, or have transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but Palau is a diving destination with limited hospital capacity — cover that includes diving accidents and medical evacuation to Guam or Manila is strongly recommended.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

onwardTicket.text: A confirmed onward or return ticket is required for the 30-day entry permit and is checked by airlines at check-in.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

proofOfFunds.text: No published amount. Immigration officers may ask where you are staying and how you will support yourself. Have your hotel booking to hand.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

declarations.name: Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee
declarations.submitWindow: Normally collected with the air ticket at the time of booking
declarations.text: Every departing visitor pays a USD 100 environmental fee that funds Palau's conservation and marine sanctuary. Airlines usually collect it inside the ticket price. Check your fare breakdown, and be ready to pay at the airport if it was not included.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

declarations.name: Arrival and customs declaration
declarations.submitWindow: Completed on the aircraft or at Roman Tmetuchl International Airport on arrival
declarations.text: An arrival card and a combined customs and biosecurity declaration are handed out on the inbound flight. Declare all food, plants and animal products.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

currencyLimits.text: Cash and other monetary instruments worth USD 10,000 or more must be declared on arrival and departure.

source.name: Republic of Palau — national government portal

notes: Reef-toxic sunscreen is banned — products containing oxybenzone, octinoxate and several related chemicals are confiscated at the airport and can carry a fine. Bring mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen instead.
Taking sea turtles, giant clams, coral or other protected marine life or souvenirs made from them is illegal.
Biosecurity is strict on fresh produce, seeds, plants and animal products.

payments.text: Palau uses the US dollar. Hotels, dive shops and larger restaurants in Koror take cards, but smaller places, taxis, state park fees and anything outside Koror are cash. Carry dollars in small notes.

safety.text: Palau has very low crime and is one of the safest destinations in the Pacific. The real risks are in the water: strong currents, deep dives far from a recompression chamber, and boat trips through the Rock Islands in changeable weather.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Palau travel information

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to April is the drier season with the calmest seas and best underwater visibility. Palau sits below the main typhoon belt but rain is possible year-round.

tips.text: On arrival, immigration stamps the Palau Pledge into your passport — a promise to the children of Palau to tread lightly — and you sign it in front of the officer. It is a required part of entry, not a souvenir, so do not refuse or deface it.
The USD 100 Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee is usually built into your airfare. Check your ticket: if it is not shown, budget for it at the airport, and keep the receipt.

Visiting the Rock Islands and Jellyfish Lake needs a separate Koror state permit, bought through your tour operator and valid for several days — commonly around USD 100 including the lake. Budget for it on top of tour prices.
Palau was the first country to ban reef-toxic sunscreen. Chemical sunscreens are taken off you at the airport — pack mineral zinc-based sunscreen, a rash guard and a hat.
Palau's dives are deep and current-swept and the nearest recompression chamber is in Koror with limited capacity. Leave at least 24 hours between your last dive and your flight out.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Palau?
faq.answer: For a normal holiday, no. Visitors of nearly every nationality are issued a free entry permit on arrival valid for 30 days, provided they hold a passport valid six months, an onward ticket and somewhere to stay. US, Micronesian and Marshallese citizens enter freely under the Compact of Free Association.

faq.question: What is the Palau Pledge?
faq.answer: It is an eco-pledge stamped into every visitor's passport at immigration, written as a promise to Palau's children to preserve the islands. You sign it on arrival in front of the officer. It takes a moment and is a condition of entry.

faq.question: How much is Palau's environmental fee?
faq.answer: The Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee is USD 100 per departing visitor and funds Palau's marine sanctuary and conservation work. Airlines normally collect it inside the ticket price when you book, so check your fare breakdown before assuming you must pay again at the airport.

faq.question: Can I stay in Palau longer than 30 days?
faq.answer: Yes. The Bureau of Immigration in Koror can extend the entry permit, generally in 30-day blocks for a fee of around USD 50 each. Apply before your current permit expires and bring your passport and onward ticket.

faq.question: Is sunscreen really banned in Palau?
faq.answer: Reef-toxic sunscreen is. Products containing oxybenzone, octinoxate and several related chemicals are prohibited, confiscated at the airport and can bring a fine for sellers. Mineral sunscreens using zinc oxide are fine and are sold locally.
